title_original: Notes from New York: The Oedipus Effect
excerpt_original: Kalshi’s entrance into the artworld has drawn much derision, but was there ever really a sacrosanct, morally upright system for it to taint?

blocks.text: The prediction market Kalshi’s entrance into the artworld has drawn much derision, but was there ever really a sacrosanct, morally upright system for it to taint?

On 2 December 2025, CNN announced a deal with Kalshi that allowed the legacy news outlet to use the online prediction market’s data on the probabilities of real-world events in their reporting. Two days later, the business news channel CNBC announced its own partnership with the so-called largest federally regulated prediction market. Writer and trend forecaster Ayesha A. Siddiqi, in an essay published earlier this year, called them, essentially, glorified cesspools for ‘insider trading’ conspiring with low-hanging news networks with ‘declining ratings and ageing demographics’. The alliances, she wrote, are ‘a mutual bid for relevance and audience’.

Artnet announced its partnership with Kalshi on 11 November 2026. It had curated, for Kalshi’s users, a selection of works among those to be auctioned at Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips later in the month. The auction outcomes could now be wagered and those wagers subsequently verified through Artnet ’s price database. Gallerists moaned and magazine editors tut-tutted as if to draw a line between themselves and their disgraced colleagues. Hundreds of Instagram commenters posted sentiments similar to Siddiqi’s. Many a vomit emoji.

Why the disgust? For one, prediction markets encourage such profanities as betting on ‘the deaths of world leaders, the bombings of countries, or the burning of forests’ and are, per author David Hill writing in The Baffler , the ‘direct descendants’ of an eighteenth-century British practice of wagering whether certain merchant ships would sink in the Atlantic or German refugees would die on the outskirts of London. When Siddiqi, Hill and journalist Jacob Silverman gathered on a panel titled ‘Bets in a Burning House’ during the annual Triple Canopy Symposium in mid-November, Hill and Silverman downplayed prediction markets as merely sportsbooks with clever marketing teams. Accordingly, Artnet ’s jaunt with Kalshi is perceived as a down-market collaboration and, moreover, tainted by the sordid stigmas of gambling and addiction. But is there really a sacrosanct, morally upright system that we can identify, against which the prediction market stands as an obscene, counterfeit Other?

blocks.caption: Triple Canopy Symposium, New York, 2026. Photo: Curtis Wallen. Courtesy Triple Canopy

blocks.text: Tuesday after the symposium, I dropped by Phillips’s Modern & Contemporary Art Evening Sale. While online speculators bet on whether smaller lots like Avery Singer’s cool grey abstraction JUUL Smoke (2021) would net above $500,000 (it did) and François-Xavier Lalanne’s zoomorphic cast-iron stove Babouin (1984) would exceed $2.5 million (it did, just), three callers were competing for Amedeo Modigliani’s Tête (1911–12), a head carved from a single block of stone à la Michelangelo. As of that morning, Kalshi’s forecast had its value at $34m. The spirit in the room was as vulgar as any betting hall, with a seated crowd of spectators, myself included, craning necks and angling phones towards the podium; it was a bidding ‘war’, after all. The ascending value of the sculpture was displayed as coldly and crudely as the odds on the prediction apps, projected behind the auctioneer in USD, EUR, GBP, CHF and HKD, beside a blindingly high resolution image of the enigmatic head posed in three-quarters profile, its flat-browed, purse-lipped smile and chiselled-out eyes evincing either pensiveness or stupidity or both. The hammer came down for $44,630,000, fees included. I left with a vague impression of having witnessed a Bataillean purge – a game that, like the prediction markets, had just created a few (presumably) satisfied winners and many sore (or indifferent) losers.

blocks.caption: Amedeo Modigliani, Tête , 1911–1912, limestone, 74 × 30 × 23 cm. Courtesy Phillips

blocks.text: The twentieth-century British philosopher Karl Popper coined the phrase ‘the Oedipus effect’ to describe the inherently self-defeating nature of social-scientific prediction. ‘Suppose, for instance, it were predicted that the price of shares would rise for three days and then fall,’ Popper writes in The Poverty of Historicism (1957). ‘Plainly, everyone connected with the market would sell on the third day, causing a fall of prices on that day and falsifying the prediction.’ Daddy issues aside, Oedipus is famous for being someone who, like the stereotypical Kalshi gambler, thinks he can outsmart the system and is ultimately done in by knowledge itself. For now, artworks on Kalshi are bringing in at most tens of thousands of dollars in trading volume, and there is no evidence that collectors bidding at auction are checking prediction platforms like augurs. But seeing as these platforms have already been influencing US politics by appearing – on CNN, for instance – in lieu of actual polling results, who’s to say online speculation won’t affect the sale price of a blue-chip lot on the Upper East Side sometime soon? I wouldn’t bet against it.

blocks.caption: Jean-Antoine-Théodore Giroust, Oedipus at Colonus , 1788, oil on canvas, 164 × 197 cm. Public domain

blocks.text: Predictions are also self-fulfilling. In Thomas Pynchon’s 1966 novella The Crying of Lot 49 , the protagonist, California housewife Oedipa Maas, loses her mind to speculation during the leadup to an auction. Oedipa increasingly suspects that a group of people are communicating with one another via an underground mail network called W.A.S.T.E., which is linked to a secret society called the Tristero. She drifts up and down California in a rental car, finding – in copious quantities – visual, verbal and written clues pointing to the existence of this shadowy organisation: graffiti on a bathroom wall, as a tattoo on a sailor’s hand, on lapel pins and bus seats. The book ends with Oedipa at the auction where the lot in question – a collection of stamps that have been altered, presumably, by the Tristero into creepy imagery like a Pony Express rider with a crooked head and a Statue of Liberty wearing a ‘faint, menacing smile’ – is to be sold to a mystery bidder, potentially also a member of the Tristero, whose identity we never learn.

In the popular imagination, the art market of the twenty-first century, like finance, has become synonymous with Tristero-level esotericism. We all already know that the secondary market operates, as art advisoer Mari-Claudia Jiménez told me in an email, “in an environment of significant information asymmetry” – in other words, that auction houses, consignors, guarantors and prospective bidders have access to information about reserves, guarantees, irrevocable bids and depth of interest in specific works that your everyday trader does not. One is not to blame, then, for being suspicious of, as Jiménez diplomatically phrased it, “conflicts of interest, misuse of confidential information and potential market manipulation”. For acting a bit paranoid. Perhaps we artworld spectators and speculators, who sit somewhere between the auction house phones and the person who clicked Kalshi’s ‘Culture’ tab by accident, could use the Oedipus effect as a thought exercise – ‘What outcomes’, we might ask ourselves, ‘ can be changed by our pronouncements and our beliefs?’ – and start imagining things from there.
